item.title: Sen. Moody Highlights Cybersecurity Push for Floridians During National Month
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: U.S. Senator Ashley Moody is using National Cybersecurity Month to highlight her legislative work protecting Floridians from online threats, including predators targeting children and scammers preying on seniors. "Criminals don't have to break into your home to steal from you—they can target you through a call, email or even a text," Moody said in…
item.content:encoded:
U.S. Senator Ashley Moody is using National Cybersecurity Month to highlight her legislative work protecting Floridians from online threats, including predators targeting children and scammers preying on seniors.

"Criminals don't have to break into your home to steal from you—they can target you through a call, email or even a text," Moody said in a statement released Tuesday. "As U.S. Senator, I'm working to protect Floridians from online bad actors—including scammers, fraudsters, and child predators."

Moody is championing several pieces of legislation. She's backing the bipartisan Kids Online Safety Act, which would give young people and parents better tools and transparency to protect against online harms—a cause she supported during her time as Florida's Attorney General. She also recently introduced the STOP Scams Against Seniors Act to help law enforcement investigate and prosecute criminals targeting seniors through fraud. Moody is an original cosponsor of the No FAKES Act, which would prevent unauthorized use of voices and images in AI-generated deepfakes, and introduced the SWIPES Act to toughen penalties on gift card fraud and close loopholes criminals exploit.

During her tenure as Florida Attorney General, Moody created the Cyber Fraud Enforcement Unit in 2023, which froze more than $17 million in illicit cryptocurrency funds and worked 40 active cases involving senior victims.

item.title: USPS Gears Up for Election Mail Delivery in 2026
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: The U.S. Postal Service says it's ready to handle ballot delivery for the 2026 election, with operations running smoothly across the country heading into the final stretch before November 3rd. Postal officials held a briefing Tuesday to outline their election mail procedures and security measures. Postmaster General David Steiner said the…
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Postal Service says it's ready to handle ballot delivery for the 2026 election, with operations running smoothly across the country heading into the final stretch before November 3rd.

Postal officials held a briefing Tuesday to outline their election mail procedures and security measures. Postmaster General David Steiner said the organization is "confident and ready to deliver a successful Election Mail season," emphasizing that the Postal Service shares a commitment with voters to ensure ballots are handled securely and delivered reliably.

The agency's long-standing advice remains the same: voters should mail completed ballots at least one week before their election office's deadline. Through early October, the Postal Service reported strong performance, with 97.98 percent of ballot mail arriving on time according to service standards. Officials also noted that extraordinary processing measures will begin October 24 at postal facilities nationwide to expedite ballot handling.

The U.S. Postal Inspection Service will work alongside the Postal Service to safeguard election mail and coordinate with election officials. In the 2024 general election, the Postal Service delivered 99.6 percent of ballots within three days of submission to election officials, according to a post-election analysis.

item.title: Pensacola Debris Removal From Hurricane Isaias Hits $16 Million, Could Take Weeks
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: The City of Pensacola is facing a massive cleanup operation in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias, with debris removal costs already climbing to an estimated $16 million as of October 19, according to city officials. The scale of the disaster is staggering. Debris hauler D&J estimates that once collection wraps up, the city will have accumulated…
item.content:encoded:
The City of Pensacola is facing a massive cleanup operation in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias, with debris removal costs already climbing to an estimated $16 million as of October 19, according to city officials.

The scale of the disaster is staggering. Debris hauler D&J estimates that once collection wraps up, the city will have accumulated roughly 1 million cubic yards of storm debris — enough to fill an entire football field stacked more than 500 feet high, or the equivalent of a 50-story building, city officials said.

The first pass of debris collection is expected to stretch 4 to 5 weeks, with the pace varying depending on conditions encountered at collection sites around the city. City spokesperson Shannon Nickinson emphasized that cleanup remains in its early stages, and those estimates could grow as the full scope of hurricane damage becomes clearer.

item.title: Construction Begins on Century Bridge Closed Since 2020
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: CENTURY, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- After more than six-and-a-half years of detours, construction has finally started on replacing Century's Freedom Road Bridge. Crews began work Monday on the bridge just east of Jefferson Avenue. The structure has been closed since Jan. 29, 2020, when inspectors discovered serious deterioration underneath the wooden…
item.content:encoded:
CENTURY, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- After more than six-and-a-half years of detours, construction has finally started on replacing Century's Freedom Road Bridge.

Crews began work Monday on the bridge just east of Jefferson Avenue.


The structure has been closed since Jan. 29, 2020, when inspectors discovered serious deterioration underneath the wooden bridge. Several pilings were no longer properly supporting the structure, with some split or severely deteriorated.


Century has spent years trying to assemble enough funding to replace it.


Florida lawmakers included $1.257 million for the project in the 2023-24 state budget, but rising construction costs delayed the work. After engineering, design and other expenses, approximately $1 million of that funding remained.


Escambia County commissioners agreed in July to contribute another $191,934 from District 5 Local Option Sales Tax discretionary funding.


Century originally awarded F&W Construction Company a contract worth more than $1.6 million. The project was subsequently reduced to approximately $1.29 million by eliminating some services and options.


Crews are beginning by relocating natural-gas, water and sewer lines currently supported by the existing bridge. Once those utilities are moved, the old structure can be demolished.

Plans call for a new 26-foot-long, single-span bridge. The project also includes roadway reconstruction, asphalt, guardrails, striping and signs.


The contractor has 280 days to complete the project, weather permitting.

The current target completion date is July 26, 2027.

item.title: Pensacola Council to Consider $695,000 Contract for Future of Former Baptist Hospital Campus
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: PENSACOLA, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Pensacola City Council could take another major step Thursday toward determining the future of the former Baptist Hospital campus. Council members will consider awarding a $695,000 one-year contract to Bayou District Consulting for development advisory services involving the large Westside property. The contract…
item.content:encoded:
PENSACOLA, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Pensacola City Council could take another major step Thursday toward determining the future of the former Baptist Hospital campus.


Council members will consider awarding a $695,000 one-year contract to Bayou District Consulting for development advisory services involving the large Westside property. The contract would not select a developer, approve construction or commit the city to any particular future use of the campus.


Instead, the firm would evaluate redevelopment options, determine what's feasible and conduct community engagement before eventually making recommendations to the city and Community Redevelopment Agency.


It's the second attempt to establish a consulting process for the property. An earlier proposal involving Bayou District Consulting was withdrawn in December 2025 following council discussion and public input.


The city subsequently restarted the process with a new request for proposals designed to increase oversight and community participation.


The revised process includes a five-member evaluation committee, including two community representatives, along with dedicated Community Engagement Lead and Community Benefits Lead positions.


Seven firms submitted proposals. Five advanced to oral presentations, with Bayou District Consulting ultimately receiving the highest score.


Paying for the contract also requires moving additional Westside CRA money.

The city currently has $300,000 allocated for the work. Another $395,000 would be shifted from funding previously designated for Westside façade grants.


Altogether, $605,000 would come from Westside Tax Increment Financing funds and $90,000 from donated proceeds.


City Council is scheduled to consider both the funding change and consulting contract during Thursday's regular meeting.


Any extension beyond the initial one-year contract would require approval from both the CRA and City Council.

item.title: Major Airport Conference Highlights Pensacola's Convention-Space Limitations
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: PENSACOLA, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Pensacola has landed a major aviation industry conference for next year, but city leaders say where the event will be held illustrates a longstanding limitation on Pensacola's ability to attract larger conventions. The Southeast Chapter of the American Association of Airport Executives will hold its 2027 annual…
item.content:encoded:
PENSACOLA, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Pensacola has landed a major aviation industry conference for next year, but city leaders say where the event will be held illustrates a longstanding limitation on Pensacola's ability to attract larger conventions.


The Southeast Chapter of the American Association of Airport Executives will hold its 2027 annual conference in the Pensacola area March 20-24.


Hundreds of airport executives, aviation professionals, consultants and industry representatives from across the Southeast are expected to attend.

Pensacola International Airport officials presented plans for the event to City Council during Monday's Agenda Conference.


Airport officials said an event of roughly 600 people essentially pushes the limits of what the area can currently accommodate in a concentrated conference setting.

Most conference activities and hotel rooms will be on Pensacola Beach. The Hilton Pensacola Beach will serve as the official conference venue, with additional room blocks at neighboring beachfront hotels.


That prompted Mayor D.C. Reeves to point out that despite Pensacola hosting the event, the conference couldn't realistically be based inside Pensacola city limits.

Reeves said Pensacola lacks the combination of concentrated hotel rooms and meeting space necessary to compete for some larger conferences. He cited the U.S. Conference of Mayors as an example of an event the city currently wouldn't qualify to host because of those limitations.


Council members connected the discussion to the longstanding regional conversation surrounding the future of the Pensacola Bay Center and convention facilities.


Airport officials said Pensacola could also potentially compete for larger American Association of Airport Executives events if the community had facilities capable of accommodating more than 1,000 attendees in a single location.


The 2027 Southeast conference will have an operating budget of approximately $800,000, funded primarily through attendee registration and sponsorships.

Registration for the Pensacola Beach conference is already underway.

item.title: Pensacola Hauls Away More Than One Million Cubic Yards of Hurricane Debris
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: PENSACOLA, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- More than one million cubic yards of vegetation left behind by Hurricane Isaias have already been hauled away in Pensacola, and city officials say the massive cleanup effort is still in its early stages. As of Monday, contractors had collected 3,236 loads containing 1,065,463 cubic yards of vegetative debris. To…
item.content:encoded:
PENSACOLA, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- More than one million cubic yards of vegetation left behind by Hurricane Isaias have already been hauled away in Pensacola, and city officials say the massive cleanup effort is still in its early stages.


As of Monday, contractors had collected 3,236 loads containing 1,065,463 cubic yards of vegetative debris.


To put that amount into perspective, the city says one million cubic yards would cover an entire football field with debris stacked more than 500 feet high — roughly the height of a 50-story building.


The cost is growing along with the debris total. Pensacola currently estimates debris-removal expenses at approximately $16 million and climbing.


Residents shouldn't assume they've been missed if debris remains outside their homes. The city expects the first collection pass alone to take four to five weeks, depending on conditions encountered by crews. At least two passes through the city are planned.


Residents should separate vegetative debris, including tree limbs and leaves, from construction and demolition materials such as fencing, furniture, carpet, plumbing materials and pieces of damaged buildings.


Collected debris is being temporarily stored at sites at Roger Scott and Goya Drive.

Pensacola has also begun reopening parks and other public facilities as debris is cleared. Fourteen parks and play spaces have reopened, although additional repairs may still be needed to fencing, lighting and other amenities.


Bayview Park, Exchange Park and Hitzman Park remained under assessment in the city's latest recovery update.


Recycling service is scheduled to resume Oct. 26. Pensacola Energy and sanitation bill deadlines have also been extended to Nov. 2.

item.title: Three Senior Pensacola State College Administrators Fired on New President's First Day
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Pensacola State College's new president began his tenure Monday with a major shakeup of the college's senior administration. Three administrators — former Pensacola Mayor Grover Robinson IV, Vice President of Academic and Student Affairs Erin Spicer and Vice President of Business Affairs Anita Kovacs — were…
item.content:encoded:
Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Pensacola State College's new president began his tenure Monday with a major shakeup of the college's senior administration.


Three administrators — former Pensacola Mayor Grover Robinson IV, Vice President of Academic and Student Affairs Erin Spicer and Vice President of Business Affairs Anita Kovacs — were terminated as J. Alex Kelly took over as Pensacola State's seventh president.

Robinson had served as the college's governmental affairs lobbyist and liaison with state lawmakers. Before joining PSC, he served as mayor of Pensacola and spent several terms representing District 4 on the Escambia County Commission.


His relationship with the college goes back much further.


Robinson served for two decades on the Pensacola State College Foundation Board of Governors, including two years as president.


Just two months ago, PSC dedicated its Student Leadership and Activities Office in honor of Robinson and his wife, Jill, recognizing the couple's longstanding support of the college.


Spicer had worked at Pensacola State since 2005 and previously served as dean of the Warrington campus and as an instructor before becoming vice president of academic and student affairs.


Kovacs served as vice president of business affairs.


The three departures came Monday, Kelly's first day leading the college.


Kelly was selected unanimously by the Pensacola State College Board of Trustees in September to succeed longtime President Ed Meadows.


Pensacola State has not publicly provided a detailed explanation for the three terminations.

The changes leave several major positions within the college's senior administration to be filled as Kelly begins his tenure.

A log truck overturned on Highway 29 at Byrneville Road Tuesday morning, creating a traffic disruption in the North Escambia area. According to local reports, the truck was attempting to turn northbound onto Highway 29 from Byrneville Road when it experienced a mechanical failure. The malfunction caused both the tractor and trailer to overturn, spilling logs across the roadway and blocking southbound traffic.

The incident occurred during morning hours, likely affecting commuters in the area. No immediate information was available about injuries or the time needed to clear the roadway and reopen traffic.

item.title: Federal appeals court upholds Escambia school book removal case ruling
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: A federal appeals court has affirmed a lower court ruling in a long-running legal dispute over book removals from Escambia County school libraries. The U.S. Court of Appeals decision, entered today, stems from a challenge brought by PEN American Center, a nonprofit advocacy group that opposed the school board's removal of titles under Florida's HB…
item.content:encoded:
A federal appeals court has affirmed a lower court ruling in a long-running legal dispute over book removals from Escambia County school libraries. The U.S. Court of Appeals decision, entered today, stems from a challenge brought by PEN American Center, a nonprofit advocacy group that opposed the school board's removal of titles under Florida's HB 1069 legislation.

The case, filed as PEN American Center, Inc. v. Escambia County School Board, has generated significant national attention as part of broader debates over book access in public schools. PEN American Center argued that the removals violated free speech and library access rights, while the school board defended its decisions under state law.

Today's appeals court judgment affirmed the previous decision in the case. The ruling represents the latest chapter in litigation that has drawn scrutiny from national free speech and education advocates. Escambia County schools and PEN American Center have not yet released statements responding to the decision.

item.title: Eleventh Circuit Rules Escambia Schools Can't Use Legislative Privilege to Block Book Removal Questions
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: A federal appeals court has ruled that the Escambia County School Board cannot invoke legislative privilege to avoid answering questions about its removal of hundreds of books from school library shelves, according to reporting from PEN America. The Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals decision clears the way for discovery and depositions in an…
item.content:encoded:
A federal appeals court has ruled that the Escambia County School Board cannot invoke legislative privilege to avoid answering questions about its removal of hundreds of books from school library shelves, according to reporting from PEN America.

The Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals decision clears the way for discovery and depositions in an ongoing case challenging the district's book removal process. The ruling represents a significant legal setback for the school board's effort to shield its deliberations about which titles to remove from libraries.

The case centers on the district's practice of removing books from school library shelves—a process that has drawn scrutiny from free speech advocates who argue it violates students' and parents' constitutional rights to access diverse reading materials.

The decision suggests courts are skeptical of attempts by public bodies to use legislative immunity as a shield against accountability in First Amendment cases involving book access. Escambia County's school board has been among the most aggressive in Florida in removing titles from libraries in recent years.

item.title: Visit Pensacola Taps Tony Lyle as New President and CEO
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Visit Pensacola has announced the appointment of Tony Lyle as its next President and CEO, effective October 26. Lyle arrives with more than 25 years of destination marketing and tourism leadership experience, most recently serving as Executive Director of Visit Galveston in Texas for the past three years. Throughout his career, Lyle has overseen…
item.content:encoded:
Visit Pensacola has announced the appointment of Tony Lyle as its next President and CEO, effective October 26. Lyle arrives with more than 25 years of destination marketing and tourism leadership experience, most recently serving as Executive Director of Visit Galveston in Texas for the past three years.

Throughout his career, Lyle has overseen multimillion-dollar public tourism budgets and led strategic initiatives at destination marketing organizations across coastal and Gulf Coast regions. His background spans leisure and group travel, sports tourism, international travel partnerships, brand development, and digital transformation. He holds a Bachelor of Education in Outdoor and Science Education from Liverpool John Moores University in the United Kingdom.

"We are thrilled to have selected Tony Lyle as our new president and CEO," said Visit Pensacola Board Chairman Sterling Gilliam. "His experience leading exceptional organizations makes him a great fit for the Visit Pensacola team, which is already performing at an impressive level."

Lyle said he's eager to collaborate with tourism partners and community leaders. "The most successful destinations are built through collaboration, trust and a shared vision for the future," he said. "I'm looking forward to listening and learning from our tourism partners, community leaders and residents, and working together to build on Pensacola's momentum while creating new opportunities for visitation and meaningful economic impact for Escambia County."

Lyle will introduce himself to the community at Visit Pensacola's Annual Meeting on Wednesday, October 28, at 11:30 a.m., and at the board meeting on Wednesday, November 18, at 3 p.m. at the Bowden Building. Those interested in scheduling a meeting with Lyle can contact Visit Pensacola Executive Assistant Sarah Samsa at ssamsa@visitpensacola.com.
